clue.text: Apparently not alone in being in a tizzy

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: standing next to your own self, so with company
second meaning: frantic, overwrought with emotion

explanation.surface: Someone flustered in company, as if their nerves came from not being on their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' flags the joke: if you are beside someone you are not alone, even when that someone is yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person so agitated or distraught that they have lost their composure entirely.

blocks.note: surface reading: a job that is depressing and saps morale
setter's reading: a man whose work is literally driving spirits out of people or places

explanation.surface: A sympathetic remark about a man stuck in a gloomy, soul-destroying job.
explanation.walkthrough: Dispiriting normally means disheartening; here it means removing spirits, as a priest casting out demons does.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person performs rites that expel evil spirits or demons from someone possessed or a haunted house.

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who brokered a political settlement in modern Greece
setter's reading: the ancient Greek goddess who personified peace

explanation.surface: Praise for a female diplomat who settled a conflict in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue sounds like modern politics, but the woman is mythological: the goddess of peace in the Greek pantheon.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek mythology she was one of the Horae, the deity personifying peace, and her name means peace in Greek.

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing sitting on another is placed below it, so the odds come after the Spanish word

blocks.note: el is the Spanish for 'the'
betting odds of one to one are called evens

explanation.surface: A betting tip on Spanish football sides.
explanation.definitionFit: Football and cricket sides consist of eleven players, so a team in those sports is called an eleven.

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upward means the short word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a timetable or list of times is a table

explanation.surface: A celebrity arriving exactly when the programme said.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable is a prominent, important person, the same kind of figure as a very important person.

clue.text: Sailor takes drink on the briny

indicators.note: the sailor takes the drink along with him, so one follows the other

blocks.note: an old salt is an experienced sailor
a drink, taken as plain water

explanation.surface: A seaman has a drink while out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The briny' is informal for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The briny is a jocular name for the ocean, whose water is salty rather than fresh.

indicators.note: one word takes the other alongside it, so they are joined end to end

blocks.note: a lot means many
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pastime that lots of people take up.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a game of chance, like bingo, where numbers are drawn and players match them on cards.

blocks.note: surface reading: a couple living together to test whether they should wed
setter's reading: a marriage is a pairing, and a pairing of teams is a contest; a trial one is a warm-up game

explanation.walkthrough: A match is both a marriage and a sporting fixture, so a trial one is a friendly rehearsal game.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an unofficial game played for training and to try out players before competitive fixtures.

clue.text: Midlands town exceptionally pleasing to man

indicators.note: exceptionally suggests out of the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written: thirteen letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A tourist puff for an English town that men find particularly delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: Leamington Spa is a Warwickshire town in the English Midlands, once famous for its healing waters.
explanation.definitionFit: This Royal spa town lies in Warwickshire in central England, the region known as the Midlands.

clue.text: US president to resolve New Deal

indicators.note: a new deal of cards redistributes them, so the letters are shuffled into fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An American leader set out to settle on a new economic programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The New Deal was Franklin Roosevelt's 1930s recovery programme, so the indicator doubles as a nod to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Two holders of the American presidency bore this surname: Theodore and Franklin Delano.

clue.text: In decimal, it represents just over 1pints

indicators.note: the answer sits in the run of words that follows, spanning their letters

blocks.note: the tail of decimal, the whole of it and the start of represents

explanation.surface: A conversion note on how a quantity is written as a decimal.
explanation.walkthrough: The source has lost a fraction: the printed clue read 'just over 1¾ pints'. The talk of decimals and conversion hides the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This metric measure of capacity equals about 1.76 imperial pints, so it is a shade above one and three-quarters.

indicators.note: sound tells us to go by how the word is spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: cash is currency, money in notes and coins

explanation.surface: Advice to stash away reliable money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like an adjective meaning safe, describing the currency, but it is the homophone signal.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to store something in a secret place, conceal it for later.

blocks.note: the elbow is the joint of the arm
a study is a room for working in

explanation.surface: Somewhere set aside for studying together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' looks like an adjective, shared, describing the study; it is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means enough room to move freely, from having space to spread your arms.

clue.text: Is set in this month's presses

indicators.note: something set in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: inst., short for instant, means of this month in old commercial letters; add the possessive S
taken as written

explanation.surface: A note about what is going into the newspapers this month.
explanation.walkthrough: Inst. is an old business-letter abbreviation for this month. 'Presses' is a verb, urges, not printing presses.
explanation.definitionFit: To press a point is to demand or maintain it firmly, so both verbs mean urge forcefully.

clue.text: Drivers aren't slow to fall into it

definitions.text: Drivers aren't slow to fall into it

blocks.clueFragment: aren't slow to fall into it
blocks.note: surface reading: motorists readily take up some habit
setter's reading: it catches the motorists who are not driving slowly, that is, the speeders

explanation.surface: A complaint that motorists are quick to adopt some bad habit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aren't slow to' sounds like 'are eager to', but it literally means motorists going too fast are the ones caught.
explanation.definitionFit: Police set up these concealed radar checks to catch motorists exceeding the limit.

indicators.note: an adjustment shifts things around, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
rain is water falling from the sky

explanation.surface: A financial change made by the water authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water board' looks like one utility company, but 'board' is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrain is to get on a train, just as you board a carriage or bus.

clue.text: Bill without a single wrong number

indicators.note: without here means outside, so one piece wraps around the other
something wrong is out of order, so these letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
taken as written

explanation.surface: An invoice that omits one incorrect figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is read as numb-er, something that numbs, not a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A painkiller deadens feeling and so numbs the patient, which makes it something that numbs.

clue.text: Are moving home; it must be serious

indicators.note: moving letters are shifted from their places into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
a nest is a home, a bird's in particular

explanation.surface: Relocating house is no laughing matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving home' reads as one phrase, relocating; 'moving' works on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An earnest person is sincere and grave in manner, lacking frivolity, hence solemn.

clue.text: Ring bell on counter where travellers have to pay

indicators.note: in a down clue the first word sits on top of the second, so it comes first

blocks.note: to toll is to ring a bell slowly
a bar is the counter in a pub

explanation.surface: Someone sounding a bell at a shop counter to pay up.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrier across a road is lifted only once a passing user has handed over the charge for using it.

indicators.note: one word lies outside the other, wrapping around it

blocks.note: curt means short, abrupt
taken as written

explanation.surface: The supply of fruit was running low out in the open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran short' reads as one phrase, ran out; the words are split.
explanation.definitionFit: This small dried seedless grape, or the berry of a ribes bush, is a common fruit.

indicators.note: one piece comes before the other, so they are joined in that order

blocks.note: CL is 150 in Roman numerals
to out someone is to put them out, dismiss them

explanation.surface: A cricketer scored 150 runs before losing his wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes 'hit' look like batting runs; it is the definition, meaning struck.
explanation.definitionFit: To clout someone is to strike them hard, usually with the hand, so the past tense means struck.

clue.text: Support, from chair, fuss about sick animal

indicators.note: about means around, so one word encloses the next

blocks.note: the arm of a chair is a support for your arm
ado means fuss
ill means sick

explanation.surface: Someone props up an ailing creature with a chair while making a fuss over it.
explanation.definitionFit: This armoured burrowing mammal of the Americas is covered in bony plates and can roll into a ball.

blocks.note: first meaning: the Latin word for mother, used in old public-school slang
second meaning, whimsical: one who mates, delivering checkmate at chess

explanation.surface: A mum who decides when the family will move house for the last time.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the second sense is invented: a 'mate-r' is a player who mates, and checkmate ends a chess game.
explanation.definitionFit: Mater is Latin for mum, and British schoolboys once used it jokingly for their parent.

blocks.note: surface reading: a man who digs trenches, so the invitation is to start excavating
setter's reading: a trencherman is a hearty eater, and the invitation is to start eating

explanation.walkthrough: A trencher was a wooden plate, so a trencherman is a big eater, though the word suggests a ditch-digger.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase is said to diners to encourage them to begin their meal heartily.

clue.text: I'd return, say, to ring James in Spain

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: I'd without its apostrophe
e.g., for example, means say
a ring is O-shaped

explanation.surface: Someone plans to go back and telephone a man called James who lives in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish form of the name derives from Santiago, Saint James, so the two names are equivalents.

indicators.note: misdirected letters are sent the wrong way, so they end up rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Tracking down a delivery that was sent to the wrong address.
explanation.definitionFit: To cater is to provide food or whatever is needed for people, the verb meaning to provide.

clue.text: Uses soft soap, as fatty stuff's increased in price

blocks.note: butter is fatty stuff, plus the possessive S
prices that have risen are up

explanation.surface: Someone sweet-talks because the price of dairy fat has gone up.
explanation.walkthrough: Soft soap is flattery; butter is the same idea, a smooth coating.
explanation.definitionFit: To flatter someone in order to win a favour is to sweet-talk them, which soft soap means.

definitions.note: a whimsical second sense: what drama students are, being trained to act

blocks.note: first meaning: determined, ready to take action
second meaning, literal: students of acting are being got ready to perform

explanation.surface: A remark on how determined theatre students are.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works as an idiom for being willing to take steps, and literally for trainee actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone willing to take decisive steps is determined, firm in purpose, ready for action.
